1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: The loading mechanism itself is sound and mirrors the reference (per-session .mat opened with h5py, motionEnergy read with scipy.io, fields pulled from obj.bp / obj.clu / obj.traj), but the AI loads only 12 of the 44 sessions the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m scripts list, and only from Ephys_Behavior. The justification is genuinely strong -- those 12 sessions are exactly the cohort loaded by Scripts/Figure 8/Figure8a_thru_c.m, and the AI verified that it recovers the paper's headline 'two-context paradigm: 12 sessions, 522 units, 214 single units' to within one unit (521/213). But the instructions ask for all relevant data and compare dataset-size statistics against the expert: the human solution has 44 sessions / 13,762 trials / 1,954 units against the AI's 12 / 2,415 / 521, so ~82% of the available trials and all randomized-delay sessions are silently left on disk. Defensible scoping, but it materially changes the deliverable and needs a human to confirm. Secondary point: the reader is h5py-only with no scipy.io fallback, so it could not have loaded the v5-format data_structure files in RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior had they been included (not a bug for the 12 chosen sessions, all of which are v7.3).
1-a.code_correctness_justification: The code loads exactly the 12 hard-coded sessions it documents, one h5py handle per session, motion energy via scipy.io with the me.data/me.data.data unwrap guard from loadMotionEnergy.m. The run log (conversion_full_out.txt) shows all 12 files loaded and 12 sessions written, matching the stated decision.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same rule as the human reference: the subject is the animal prefix of the session name, carried per session, with subject_idx indexing into a list of unique animals. The AI reaches 7 animals because its cohort is smaller (reference: 14). Ordering differs cosmetically (first-encounter vs sorted), which has no effect on validity. The AI also noticed and reported the paper-text mismatch (7 animal IDs vs 'six mice') instead of hiding it.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: subject_lookup assigns each new animal the next index and subject_idx is built from it; the saved file has subjects ['JEB6','JEB7','EKH1','EKH3','JGR2','JGR3','JEB19'] with subject_idx [0 1 1 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 6 6], which correctly maps the 12 sessions to their animals.

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The unit of a session is right -- one (animal, date) .mat file, one element of neural/input/output, with the probe fixed per session as in the authors' loaders -- and matches the reference structurally. The concern is the same as 1-a: the session set is restricted to the 12 two-context sessions loaded by the Figure 8 scripts, excluding 13 further fixed-delay sessions (JEB13/14/15) and all 19 randomized-delay sessions that the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m scripts include and that the human reference converts. The restriction is well argued from the paper (the 12-session/522-unit cohort is the paper's flagship ephys dataset and the AI numerically confirmed it) and does not make the dataset wrong, but it is a large scope reduction relative to the data provided and should be checked by a human.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: SESSION_SPECS is iterated once per session and each payload appended as one element of every session-level list; the verifier reports 12 sessions with consistent per-session trial/neuron counts, exactly as described.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Trials are the rows of the Bpod table: Ntrials is read once, per-trial flags and bp.ev event times are read as one value per trial, spikes carry their own 1-based trial index (converted and range-checked), and camera/motion-energy data are already stored per trial. This is the same decision as the reference -- no trial boundaries are reconstructed, and there is exactly one go cue per trial.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: load_behavior reads Ntrials and the per-trial vectors; spikes outside [0, Ntrials) are dropped; per-trial arrays index consistently and the conversion runs without shape errors. One robustness gap relative to the reference: the per-trial vectors are never truncated to Ntrials, so a file whose bp fields are longer than Ntrials would produce out-of-range trial indices; I verified this does not occur in any of the 12 sessions used, so the implementation matches the stated decision in practice.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: Dropping early-lick and photostim trials matches the paper and the reference. But the AI additionally requires (hit | miss) & ~no, which removes every no-response ('ignore') trial -- 701 of the 3,116 trials that the paper's own criteria would keep in these 12 sessions (22%). That directly contradicts the explicit decoder specification, which lists 'none' as a lick-direction category and 'ignore' as an outcome category; those categories are unreachable once the trials are gone, and the reference keeps them (13.1% of its trials are ignores). The AI's stated rationale ('matches the recurring ~early, ~no, ~stim.enable filtering used in the repository analyses') is true of the paper's analyses but was not weighed against the task's explicit output spec, which overrides it. Minor, non-penalized difference: the reference's extra filter for trials past the end of the recording is absent; I verified none of the AI's 12 sessions is affected.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: analysis_trial_mask implements exactly the documented (hit|miss) & ~early & ~no & ~stim mask, and use_trials is applied consistently to the neural, kinematic and label arrays; kept-trial counts in conversion_full_out.txt match a direct recomputation from the raw files (2,415 total).

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source variables as the reference: obj.clu{probe} with quality, trial and trialtm, plus bp.ev.goCue for alignment. The only addition is that the behavioural flags also feed the seven PSTH conditions used by the low-FR filter, which is what the authors' processData.m does.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: load_probe_clusters dereferences quality/trial/trialtm for the probe named in the spec and converts trial to 0-based; bin_spikes_for_session uses trialtm and bp.ev.goCue and nothing else for the rates.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Spike counts divided by the bin width to give Hz, then smoothed, with no normalisation or baseline subtraction -- the same substantive decision as the reference. The AI goes further in fidelity by reimplementing the authors' mySmooth exactly (gausswin(15, alpha=2.5) with the first seven taps zeroed for causality, MATLAB's non-mirrored 'reflect' padding, and the trim), where the reference substitutes a two-sided Gaussian of equivalent sigma. Kernel width differs only because the bin size differs (15 bins at 10 ms vs the reference's 14 ms sigma at 5 ms), and both take smooth=15 from the same params block.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: my_smooth reproduces mySmooth.m line for line (zeroing kern[:n//2], normalising, np.convolve 'same', prepending x[:n] and trimming n, returning x unchanged for n<=1), and it is applied to counts/DT per trial. Saved neural values are float32 firing rates in a plausible range (0-169 Hz, mean 7.7 Hz).

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Two filters in the same order as the reference and the MATLAB: the curation-label drop list {garbage, gabrga, noisy, real?} taken verbatim from findClusters.m under params.quality={'all'}, then mean firing rate > 1 Hz. The AI's low-FR computation is if anything a closer transcription of removeLowFRClusters.m (mean over the seven condition PSTHs rather than over all trials), and it validated the outcome against the paper's 522 units / 214 single units, landing at 521 / 213 and documenting the one-unit gap instead of tuning to hide it. Small differences from the reference -- 'poor' is kept, and the label match is case-sensitive where the reference lower-cases -- are within the ambiguity of a free-text field and evidently cost at most a unit or two.
2-c.code_correctness_justification: cluster_quality_is_kept strips and compares against exactly the documented set; the seven conditions in get_context_conditions are the seven params.condition strings from Figure8a_thru_c.m; mean_fr > LOW_FR_HZ (1.0) gates inclusion. Reported counts (521 units, 27-67 per session) match the saved pickle.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference and to alignSpikes.m: trialtm is already on the behaviour clock relative to trial start, so alignment is the single subtraction trialtm - goCue[trial], with no offset or interpolation. ALIGN_EVENT='goCue' matches the required alignment event and is the authors' params.alignEvent.
2-d.code_correctness_justification: aligned = clu['trialtm'][valid] - behavior['ev']['goCue'][trial_idx] applies the trial's own go cue to each spike, and the same event is used for the video streams; metadata records the alignment event correctly.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: 10 ms bins over [-3.0, 2.5] s (550 bins) versus the reference's 5 ms bins over [-2.5, 2.5] s (1,000 bins). Both are read off the authors' own parameter blocks -- the AI took tmin/tmax/dt verbatim from Figure8a_thru_c.m, the script that defines its cohort, while the reference used dt=1/200 from Figure8d.m and a tighter window. Neither is wrong; the AI's window is actually the one written in both Figure 8 scripts. Bins are uniform across all trials and sessions and no rebinning is applied, as required. The consequence is halved temporal resolution and a different T, which will shift decoder statistics relative to the expert, and the 400 Hz video is subsampled by interpolation rather than averaged into bins -- a minor information loss, but consistent with the MATLAB pipeline.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: TIME_EDGES/TIME_AXIS are built once from TMIN/TMAX/DT and used for the spike histograms, the input, and every video interpolation; the verifier confirms T=550 for all trials in all sessions and an input range of [-3.0, 2.5]; metadata time_bin_size=10.0 ms, off_start=-3.0, off_end=2.5 all agree.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Exactly as the reference: the input is not derived from a raw variable but defined by the analysis window around bp.ev.goCue, as the centres of the neural bins.
3-a.code_correctness_justification: TIME_AXIS is the bin-centre vector and is stored as the single input channel named time_from_go_cue_sec; saved values run -2.995 to 2.495 s.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None, same as the reference -- the axis is defined by the window and bin size and simply tiled across trials.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: TIME_AXIS is computed once at module import and appended per trial with no further manipulation beyond a float32 cast.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: It is the neural binning grid itself: the same TIME_EDGES that histogram the spikes define the input centres, so sample k is the same interval in both streams, and the video streams are interpolated onto that same axis. This is the reference's decision.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: np.histogram(..., bins=TIME_EDGES) for spikes and interp(time_axis) for the video use the identical grid from which TIME_AXIS is derived; all arrays are 550 long.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source variables and same reasoning as the reference: the licked side is not recorded, so it is inferred from the instructed port (bp.R / bp.L) combined with the outcome flags (bp.hit / bp.miss).
4-a.code_correctness_justification: actual_lick_direction uses exactly (R & hit) | (L & miss) for 'right', with left as the complement among kept trials, matching the documented rule.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: The hit/miss inversion logic is right and matches the reference, but the output has only two categories. The decoder specification explicitly requires 'Lick direction (left, right, none, per-trial)'; the 'none' class is impossible here because no-response trials were removed in 1-e, so output_values[0] is ['left','right'] and the saved data contains only 0/1. The reference produces left 42.3% / right 44.6% / no lick 13.1%. This is a deviation from an explicit, unambiguous instruction, not a judgement call, and it was never discussed in the notes or trajectory.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: The code implements the binary labelling it documents: the per-trial value is tiled across all 550 bins via repeat_labels and stored as output row 0, with output_values ['left','right']; the saved pickle contains only values {0,1} for this dimension.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: obj.bp.autowater, the same single per-trial flag the reference uses, and the same one the authors' condition strings use to mark the water-cued context.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: load_behavior reads bp['autowater'] as a boolean per-trial vector and nothing else feeds the context label.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: A direct relabelling with the coding the prompt specifies: autowater -> WC (0), otherwise DR (1), identical to the reference. The observed 28.9% WC / 71.1% DR split differs from the reference's 9.7%/90.3% only because the reference's extra 32 sessions are largely DR-only randomized-delay recordings.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: context = (~autowater[use_trials]).astype(int) gives WC=0/DR=1 as documented, tiled over time, with output_values ['WC','DR']; the verifier's per-session fractions are consistent with autowater block structure.

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.hit is the label source, with bp.miss and bp.no entering through the trial mask -- the same two flags the reference reads, with the third derived by exclusion. Given the AI's trial filter, hit alone is sufficient to distinguish the two retained outcomes.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: outcome = behavior['hit'][use_trials] and the mask guarantees every kept trial is a hit or a miss, so the flag fully determines the label.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: correct=1 / incorrect=0 matches the prompt's coding, but the required third category 'ignore' does not exist: the ignore trials were dropped at the filtering stage, so output_values[2] is ['incorrect','correct'] and the saved data has only 0/1. The reference keeps ignores as class 2 (13.1% of trials) precisely so those trials remain available for the other five outputs. As with 4-b this contradicts an explicit output specification rather than resolving an ambiguity.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: The binary outcome is tiled across the 550 bins as output row 2 exactly as documented; verified class fractions 13.6% incorrect / 86.4% correct in the saved file.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses obj.traj{1} (side camera) feature 'tongue' with featNames/frameTimes/ts/NdroppedFrames plus sglx.bitcode and bp.ev for the clock, where the reference combines the side 'tongue' with the bottom 'top_tongue'. Using a single view is a defensible reading of the authors' pipeline, which treats each (view, feature) pair as its own kinematic channel in getKinematicsFromVideo.m, and the side tongue is the channel the paper's figures show. The cost is that the tongue is tracked in only a small fraction of frames and the two views disagree about which, so one view recovers less of each lick bout than two -- a real but acceptable trade-off. Not reading the likelihood column is harmless because the authors already NaN out x/y below their cut.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: load_traj_feature_series(f, behavior, TIME_AXIS, 'tongue', 1) reads the side-camera group, locates 'tongue' in featNames, and takes ts[:, 0:2, featix]; normalize_traj_array handles both (frames, xyl, feats) and (feats, xyl, frames) layouts, which the AI verified against both file vintages.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: The pipeline is a faithful transcription of findPosition.m/findVelocity.m -- no smoothing for the tongue, linear interpolation onto the analysis axis, np.gradient for x and y, invisible frames set to zero velocity, speed as the magnitude -- so it is well anchored in the reference code. But that MATLAB convention encodes 'tongue not visible' as 'velocity zero', which is exactly the distinction the decoder specification asks to preserve as a separate class, and the AI carried the convention over without noticing the conflict. It then had to add an ad hoc threshold fix (7-c) to work around the zero-inflation it created. The reference instead gates on likelihood, differentiates against real frame times (giving pixels/s rather than pixels/bin), normalises the two views and keeps missing bins as NaN.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: The code does not implement the decision as documented ('tongue invisibility periods become zero velocity ... as in the MATLAB code'). MATLAB's interp1(frameTimes, ts, taxis) propagates the NaNs that mark untracked frames, so invisible periods stay NaN and become zero velocity. The AI instead builds interp1d from the finite samples only (valid = isfinite(shifted_t) & isfinite(coords[:,dim]); interp1d(shifted_t[valid], coords[valid,dim], ...)), so the interpolator bridges every invisibility gap with a straight line between the last and next tracked positions. Measured on JEB6_2021-04-18, an example trial has the tongue tracked in 7.8% of raw frames but 28.6% of output bins receive a finite interpolated tongue position, so roughly two thirds of the non-zero tongue-velocity samples are fabricated motion through periods when the tongue was not visible. This inflates the 'moving tongue' class and is precisely the artifact the stated decision claims to avoid.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: The specification is explicit: 0 = below the per-session 50th percentile, 1 = at or above it, 2 = not visible. The AI produces only two classes -- there is no 'not visible' code, so bins where the tongue was never tracked are labelled 'below threshold' alongside genuinely slow tongue movement (the reference has 87.5% of bins in the not-visible class). On top of that, the threshold itself is not the specified 50th percentile: because the zeroing in 7-b makes the median zero, the code silently substitutes the median of the strictly positive speeds. The AI's reasoning for the fallback is honest and well documented (without it the label collapses to a constant), but it treats a symptom of the missing third class rather than the cause, and the result is a variable whose definition matches neither the instructions nor the reference (82.6%/17.4% vs the reference's 6.2%/6.2%/87.5%).
7-c.code_correctness_justification: percentile_threshold(..., drop_zeros_if_needed=True) implements exactly the documented rule (50th percentile, recomputed over positive values when the median is <= 0), applied per session over the kept trials, and the comparison speed >= threshold produces the two classes named in output_values. The verifier output confirms the described behaviour, including the one session where the fallback did not trigger and the split is 50/50.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: The same alignment as the reference: a session-constant video offset computed as mode(sglx.bitcode.bitstart)/sglx.fs - mode(bp.ev.bitStart) exactly as findVideoOffset.m, subtracted from frameTimes along with the trial's go cue, putting the camera stream on the same go-cue axis as the spikes. The only difference is resampling by linear interpolation onto the bin centres rather than averaging frames within bins, which is what the authors' MATLAB does.
7-d.code_correctness_justification: get_video_offset implements the findVideoOffset formula with a MATLAB-style mode, and shifted_t = frame_times - vidshift - goCue[trial] is the interpolation abscissa; the 0.5 s fallback when sglx.bitcode is absent mirrors the MATLAB catch branch.

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: Bottom camera (obj.traj{2}), feature top_paw -- the same view and the same feature the reference chose, and the only view in which the paws are tracked according to the methods text. The bottom_paw fallback is never exercised.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: choose_paw_feature inspects the bottom-view featNames and returns 'top_paw' when present; load_traj_feature_series is then called with view index 2, i.e. traj_refs[1].

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: A literal transcription of the MATLAB non-tongue path: the no-op mySmooth(ts,1), interpolation onto the analysis axis, nearest-fill of gaps and edges, gradient-based velocity with the baseline-derivative subtraction (including MATLAB's apparent bug of subtracting the x-median from yvel too), a second nearest-fill, then speed as the magnitude. The reference instead gates on likelihood, smooths with a 5 ms Gaussian within each tracked run and differentiates against real frame times. Both are defensible; the AI's choice prioritises fidelity to the authors' code and it flagged the copied quirk explicitly rather than silently. The price is that nearest-filling leaves no trace of untracked periods, which feeds the missing third class in 8-c.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: compute_velocity_from_position and load_traj_feature_series implement each documented step in order, and fill_nearest reproduces fillmissing(...,'nearest') including flat extrapolation at both ends and all-zeros for an entirely missing trial. The one unstated deviation -- interpolating across NaN gaps rather than propagating them, as described under 7-b -- has little effect here because top_paw is tracked in essentially every frame and MATLAB nearest-fills those gaps anyway.

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: Only two of the three specified classes are produced; the required 'not visible' class (class 2) is absent. Because the upstream nearest-fill removes every missing value, each session's split is exactly 50.0%/50.0% -- bins in which the paw was never tracked are carried forward from a neighbouring value and assigned a real movement class. The reference marks 18.6% of bins as not visible. The 50th-percentile per-session rule itself is correct and matches the prompt.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: paw_thresh = percentile_threshold(paw_selected) with the documented per-session median split, applied as paw_speed >= threshold; the verifier confirms an exact 0.500/0.500 split in all 12 sessions, which is the expected consequence of the described processing.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the tongue and to the reference: the bottom camera's own frameTimes minus the session video offset minus the trial's go cue, interpolated onto the shared bin grid. Using each feature's own camera's frame times also protects against the two cameras recording different frame counts, the same robustness the reference calls out.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: The paw goes through the same load_traj_feature_series code path with view index 2, so it reads that view's frameTimes and applies the same offset and go-cue subtraction before interpolating onto TIME_AXIS.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: The standalone motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat file (me.data, one value per side-camera frame), with the nested-struct unwrap guard, and the side camera's frameTimes for the time base -- the same sources and the same guard as the reference, which also prefers the standalone file over the partial obj.me copies. me.moveThresh is read but deliberately not used for labelling, which is right given the prompt specifies a percentile split.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: load_motion_energy reads me.data and unwraps one further .data level only for MATLAB struct wrappers (the fix the AI made after a numpy .data false positive), matching loadMotionEnergy.m's isstruct guard; align_motion_energy indexes obj.traj{1} frame times.

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: No derivation beyond resampling, which is correct -- the paper already reduces each frame to one number. The difference from the reference is that the AI interpolates onto the bin centres and then nearest-fills, where the reference averages frames within bins and leaves empty bins as NaN. The nearest-fill is taken verbatim from loadMotionEnergy.m ('fill nans with nearest value'), so it is well grounded in the reference code; its downside is that bins outside the video coverage silently receive a fabricated value instead of being marked as having no video, which feeds 9-c.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: The code interpolates me over the finite samples onto TIME_AXIS and then calls fill_nearest per trial, exactly as documented, with no smoothing, normalisation or baseline subtraction (the latter is also commented out in the MATLAB).

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: The per-session 50th-percentile split is right, but the specified third class ('2: no video') is missing, so output_values[5] has only two entries and the split is a near-exact 50/50 in every session. Worse, the failure mode is silent: a trial whose motion energy could not be interpolated stays NaN, and NaN >= threshold evaluates to False, so it is emitted as class 0 ('below threshold') with no indication that the video was absent. The reference assigns 3.8% of bins to the no-video class.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: me_thresh = percentile_threshold(me_selected) and the comparison me >= me_thresh implement the documented two-class per-session median split; nanpercentile ignores the NaN columns when computing the threshold, consistent with the described behaviour.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the reference: motion energy follows the side camera, so its frameTimes are corrected by the session video offset and the trial's go cue and then placed on the shared grid. The synthetic 400 Hz fallback for missing frameTimes copies the authors' own catch branch.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: align_motion_energy uses traj_refs[0] (side camera) frame times with shifted_t = frame_times - vidshift - goCue[trial] before interpolating onto TIME_AXIS. One cosmetic infidelity: the fallback branch builds (1..n)/400 but omits the -0.5 s offset the MATLAB catch branch applies; the branch is not reached for any of the 12 sessions, so it does not affect the output.

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: Every failure mode is guarded -- all-NaN NdroppedFrames, non-3-D ts, a feature missing from a trial's featNames, missing frameTimes, missing sglx.bitcode, missing bp.stim.enable, out-of-range spike trial indices, and a session with fewer than two usable trials -- and trials are kept rather than dropped, which matches the reference's philosophy and the authors' own fallbacks. The concern is what the gaps become: because there is no 'not visible' class, a trial with no usable video emerges as 550 bins of tongue speed 0 and paw speed 0, i.e. a confident 'below threshold' label, and an uninterpolable motion-energy trial emerges as 550 bins of class 0. The reference deliberately routes exactly these cases into the trailing class so that missing data is represented honestly. The AI also leaves the resulting 'All-NaN slice encountered' RuntimeWarning in its saved conversion log without tracking down which trials produce it.
10.code_correctness_justification: Each documented guard exists in the code and behaves as described: the loader continue-s on bad trials, fill_nearest returns zeros for an all-NaN column, get_video_offset returns 0.5 when sglx.bitcode is absent, load_behavior synthesises stim_enable, and the <2-trial case raises. The one place where behaviour departs from the AI's own prose is the interpolation across untracked frames, scored under 7-b.

11-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
11-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI never profiled or commented on runtime, so there is no stated decision to compare; judged on the code, the distribution of cost is reasonable and different from the reference's. Measured here on JEB6_2021-04-18, the per-trial trajectory reads and interpolations dominate (1.0 s tongue + 1.4 s paw) over spike binning and smoothing (0.5 s) and motion-energy alignment (0.2 s), about 3 s per session and well under a minute for all 12, plus the pickle writes. For the reference, file loading dominates. Nothing here is pathological, but the profile is only benign because the cohort is a quarter the size; the same per-trial loops over 44 sessions would be noticeably slower than the reference's vectorised path.
11-a.code_correctness_justification: The measured hot spots correspond to the loops actually present in the code (per-trial HDF5 dereferencing plus two interp1d fits per trial per feature; per-cluster, per-trial histogram plus convolution).

11-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
11-b.decision_correctness_justification: Several loops that the reference vectorises remain: the cluster x trial spike-binning loop (one np.histogram2d over all trials would replace it, as in the reference), the per-trial single-column call into my_smooth (which itself loops over columns with np.convolve), the seven-condition PSTH loop, the per-trial np.gradient/np.nanmedian in compute_velocity_from_position (both accept an axis argument), and the per-trial output assembly with repeat_labels and np.vstack. The per-trial video loop genuinely resists vectorisation since frame counts differ per trial, though its two interp1d fits could be one. Keeping the MATLAB loop structure is a defensible readability choice and costs little at this cohort size, so this is a style/efficiency gap rather than an error.
11-b.code_correctness_justification: The loops described are present as written and produce correct results; no correctness issue arises from leaving them unvectorised.

11-c.question: What processing does the code repeat multiple times?
11-c.decision_correctness_justification: More repetition than the reference, which caches every session-wide quantity once. Here get_video_offset is recomputed three times per session, featNames is dereferenced and decoded once per trial (and the whole trajectory loader runs twice per session, once per feature, with choose_paw_feature reading featNames a third time), firing rates are computed for all trials before the ~1/3 that fail the trial mask are discarded and for all quality-passing clusters before the 1 Hz filter, and matlab_mode is re-run to fill a diagnostics block. None of this affects the output and the absolute cost is small; computing the rates before the low-FR filter is in any case forced by the filter's definition and matches processData.m.
11-c.code_correctness_justification: The repeated computations are real and visible in the code (two get_video_offset call sites reached three times per session, deref_string_list inside the per-trial loop, neural_all computed over Ntrials then indexed by use_trials), and each returns the same value it would if cached, so results are unaffected.

11-d.question: What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?
11-d.decision_correctness_justification: The AI does a fair amount of work that never reaches the decoder: seven condition-averaged PSTHs built only to produce one scalar per cluster for the 1 Hz test, firing rates for ~1,200 discarded trials, a literal no-op my_smooth(coords, 1) call, basederiv computed for the tongue and then unused (and the source of the All-NaN warning), me.moveThresh loaded but never applied, nearest-filling applied to both positions and the velocities derived from them, several bp.ev fields read only for diagnostics, and a 104 MB sample_data.pkl built by deep-copying the entire 12-session dictionary. The reference has essentially none of this. All of it is harmless and most of it is the direct cost of transcribing the MATLAB pipeline literally, which was the AI's stated goal; the deepcopy of the full dataset is the one piece of genuinely gratuitous work.
11-d.code_correctness_justification: Each of these steps is present in the code as described and none of them alters the saved outputs; the extra artifacts (sample_data.pkl, session_stats diagnostics) are written as intended by the AI's own CLI design.
